title: Chapter 57 — The Consolidation Playbook
intro: Converting split accounts into sole-source relationships — the consolidation strategy and execution.

sections.title: Why Accounts Split
sections.content:
A builder using you for half their projects and a competitor for the other half is a split account. Split accounts exist for specific reasons: the competitor carries a brand you do not, their delivery is faster for certain project types, their trade rep has a personal relationship, or they offer better pricing on specific categories.

You cannot consolidate an account until you understand why it is split. Ask directly: 'I appreciate the business you give us. I would love to earn more of it. What would need to change for you to consolidate everything with us?'

The answer is your action plan.

sections.title: The Consolidation Offer
sections.content:
Once you know the gap, address it specifically. If it is pricing: 'If you commit to running all your projects through us, I can offer you tier-two pricing across the board.' If it is a brand gap: 'I have added [brand] to our lineup — let me show you what we can do.' If it is service: 'I have restructured our trade desk to give you a dedicated delivery window on Tuesdays and Thursdays.'

Make the consolidation offer tangible. Not 'we will do better.' Specifically what changes and what they gain.

sections.title: The Volume Commitment
sections.content:
Consolidation works both ways. You offer better pricing or service. They commit to volume. Structure it formally: 'If you commit to running 80 percent or more of your appliance volume through us for the next 12 months, I will lock in tier-two pricing and priority delivery scheduling. We will review quarterly.'

A formal commitment creates accountability on both sides and makes the relationship more durable than a handshake agreement.
